summary: Slice 023C presents 1 MAJ, 2 MIN, and 1 nit safety-bypass finding. MAJ-SAFE-001 (critical path): the `expected_scp_workflow_ref` JSON Schema regex allows any owner/repo namespace — not only `jrnb2024/standards-control-plane` — so an adopter can PR a registry entry pointing to a workflow they control, causing `gh attestation verify --signer-workflow` to accept a genuine-but-adversary-owned OIDC attestation. CODEOWNERS single-operator review is the sole gate; there is no schema-level or runtime namespace enforcement. This is a missing defence-in-depth layer in the trust model's core invariant. All other safety properties are strongly upheld: `yaml.safe_load` prevents YAML-RCE, `subprocess.run` with arg-list prevents shell injection, dual `additionalProperties: false` schema enforcement on both the emit schema and the index schema eliminates waiver-content leakage, the two-job permission split is minimal, the commit job opens a PR (not push-to-main), and CODEOWNERS covers all critical paths. MIN-SAFE-002 flags the absence of an `scp_version` minimum-bound check; MIN-SAFE-003 flags inconsistent stderr truncation limits (500 vs 400 chars) across error paths. nit-SAFE-004 flags the missing job-level timeout.

findings.claim: The `expected_scp_workflow_ref` JSON Schema regex accepts any `owner/repo` namespace, not only the SCP source repository. An adopter can PR a registry entry whose `expected_scp_workflow_ref` points to a workflow they fully control. The aggregator will call `gh attestation verify --signer-workflow <adopter-workflow>` and that call will SUCCEED because GitHub's OIDC system genuinely attests that the artifact was produced by the adopter's own workflow. The OIDC verification step therefore provides zero binding to the SCP reusable workflow when the registry ref is adversarially authored. CODEOWNERS is the only gate.
findings.evidence: schemas/scorecard-opt-in-registry.schema.json line 35: pattern `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/\.github/workflows/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.ya?ml@[0-9a-f]{40}$`. The first two capture groups `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+` match any owner/repo pair — the strings `evil-org/evil-repo`, `adopter/their-repo`, and `jrnb2024/standards-control-plane` all satisfy the pattern identically. The aggregator at scorecard-aggregator.yml lines 213-224 passes `expected_workflow_ref` (read verbatim from the registry) to `gh attestation verify --signer-workflow`. Attack path: adopter PRs opt-in-registry.yaml with `expected_scp_workflow_ref: evil-org/evil-repo/.github/workflows/emit.yml@<sha>`; evil-org/evil-repo runs a workflow that uploads a crafted scorecard-emit.json (passing schema validation since they author it to conform); GitHub OIDC signs the artifact as produced by `evil-org/evil-repo/.github/workflows/emit.yml@<sha>`; aggregator calls `gh attestation verify --signer-workflow evil-org/evil-repo/...` → SUCCESS; schema-validated adversarial emit is passed through into the signed index. The bypass succeeds if the single operator (@jrnb2024) approves the registry PR without recognising the non-SCP workflow namespace.
findings.impact: If the operator approves a registry PR containing a non-SCP `expected_scp_workflow_ref` (through social engineering, cognitive load, or error), the trust model's core invariant — that only SCP-reusable-workflow-produced emits reach the index — is completely defeated. The adversarial adopter controls: `verdict` (can force `allow`), `rule_counts` (can suppress all deny counts), `waivers_aggregate` (can inflate active_count), and `scp_version` (can claim any version). The resulting index row is indistinguishable from a legitimate verified row. The index is CODEOWNERS-gated at merge time, but the operator reviewing the aggregator PR sees only the aggregated index diff (counts, verdicts), not the raw emit provenance — so a single-point-of-failure in the registry PR review translates directly to a signed-index integrity failure.
findings.mitigation: Apply both controls for defence-in-depth. (1) Schema-level: anchor the `expected_scp_workflow_ref` pattern to the SCP source namespace — change the pattern in schemas/scorecard-opt-in-registry.schema.json to `^jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/\.github/workflows/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.ya?ml@[0-9a-f]{40}$`. Add a schema `$comment` noting the pattern must be updated if the repository is renamed or transferred (file TF-023C-005 to track that decision). (2) Runtime-level: add a namespace prefix check in the aggregator Python script (scorecard-aggregator.yml) before the `gh attestation verify` call — e.g., `if not expected_workflow_ref.startswith('jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/.github/workflows/'): row['status'] = 'verification_failure'; row['error'] = 'expected_scp_workflow_ref does not reference SCP source namespace'; adopter_rows.append(row); continue`. This provides defence-in-depth against a schema change or human review lapse.

findings.claim: There is no automated minimum-version check on the `scp_version` field of the verified emit. An adopter can legitimately pin `expected_scp_workflow_ref` to an old SCP commit SHA (predating the scorecard-emit security baseline in v1.2.0), and the aggregator will accept emits claiming `scp_version: 1.0.0` or earlier. The operator must manually identify during the registry PR review that the SHA corresponds to an acceptably recent SCP release, with no tooling support.
findings.evidence: scorecard-aggregator.yml lines 250-257: `row['scp_version'] = emit.get('scp_version', '')` — the value is passed through without comparison to any minimum bound. The emit schema (scorecard-emit.schema.json line 34) enforces semver format `^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$` but no `minimum` version constraint. The registry schema enforces a 40-char hex SHA but no recency or version-baseline check. Dispatch note §risk.2 identifies SHA-pin drift as a risk but only in the context of adopters bumping forward (Renovate); the backward-pin scenario (adopter registers an old SHA) is unaddressed. An emit produced by SCP v1.1.x (before scorecard-emit was introduced in 023B / v1.2.0) would fail schema validation only if the emit format itself diverged — a pre-v1.2.0 SCP run would not produce a scorecard-emit artifact at all, resulting in `no_emit` status. However, a SHA pinning to any commit between v1.2.0 and the current HEAD is fully accepted with no freshness signal.
findings.impact: Low at current estate size (no adopters yet). At scale, adopters on very old SCP SHAs could have weaker schema enforcement (e.g., pre-023C schema changes), different waiver-count semantics, or absent security fixes in the emit-producing step. The `scp_version` field is informational in the index and is not validated for minimum version by any downstream consumer (023D, 023E). Operator visibility is limited to the `scp_version` column in the markdown report (023D, not yet implemented).
findings.mitigation: File TF-023C-003. Short-term: document in `docs/scorecards/opt-in-registry.yaml` header that `expected_scp_workflow_ref` SHA MUST correspond to an SCP release >= v1.2.0, and that the operator verifying the registry PR must confirm this. Medium-term: add a `min_scp_version` field to the registry schema (optional; informational) and a runtime check in the aggregator: `from packaging.version import Version; if Version(emit['scp_version']) < Version('1.2.0'): row['status'] = 'verification_failure'; ...`. The `packaging` library is in the policy-check.txt requirements lockfile.

findings.claim: The stderr truncation limit is inconsistent across the three subprocess error paths: `gh run list` failures truncate at 500 chars (scorecard-aggregator.yml line 159) while `gh run download` and `gh attestation verify` failures truncate at 400 chars (lines 196, 229). No sanitisation removes ANSI escape codes or control characters from stderr before interpolation into the error string. The longest path (500 chars) exposes 25% more gh CLI stderr than the others. gh CLI stderr for rate-limited or auth-failed API calls can include GitHub API JSON response bodies containing operational metadata.
findings.evidence: scorecard-aggregator.yml line 159: `result.stderr.strip()[:500]` for gh run list failures. Line 196-198: `download.stderr.strip()[:400]` for gh run download failures. Line 229: `verify.stderr.strip()[:400]` for gh attestation verify failures. Line 244: `str(e)[:400]` for jsonschema/json errors. The `.strip()` call removes leading/trailing whitespace but not embedded ANSI escape sequences (e.g., `\x1b[31m`) or control characters that gh CLI may emit to terminal-like outputs. These are embedded in the index's `error` string and committed to git. No GH_TOKEN or credential is passed as a CLI argument (token is via GH_TOKEN env), so token leakage via stderr is not a risk.
findings.impact: Low. CODEOWNERS-reviewed PR must be merged before the error strings reach the signed index on main. Operational metadata (rate limit windows, repo visibility hints, API error codes) could be exposed to index consumers at 023D/023E. Control characters in error strings could cause rendering issues in the markdown report generator (023D). The primary risk is cosmetic and operational, not a security bypass.
findings.mitigation: Normalise all four error paths to a single 400-char truncation limit (already used in three of four paths). Add a sanitisation pass before interpolation: `stderr_safe = re.sub(r'\x1b\[[0-9;]*m', '', result.stderr).strip()[:400]` to strip ANSI codes. One-line fix per error site; use a shared helper function to avoid future drift.

findings.claim: The `aggregate` job has no `timeout-minutes` constraint. With N opted-in adopters, worst-case job duration is N × 180 seconds (three sequential subprocess calls each with a 60-second timeout). At N=40 adopters, worst case is 2 hours; at N=120, it approaches GitHub Actions' 6-hour job limit. No per-adopter circuit breaker halts the job early if the aggregate duration budget is exceeded.
findings.evidence: scorecard-aggregator.yml jobs.aggregate: no `timeout-minutes` key. Python subprocess calls at lines 136-155 (gh run list, timeout=60), 179-200 (gh run download, timeout=60), 213-236 (gh attestation verify, timeout=60). The adopter list is bounded only by CODEOWNERS-approved registry entries, so a sufficiently large estate could cause the aggregate job to run for hours if all adopters have slow or unresponsive API endpoints.
findings.mitigation: File TF-023C-004. Add `timeout-minutes: 30` to the aggregate job for near-term safety (caps at current small-N scale). Plan an adopter-count circuit breaker at 023E: if `len(adopters_in) > MAX_ADOPTERS`, emit a workflow warning and process only the first MAX_ADOPTERS entries alphabetically, with the remainder recorded as `no_emit` with a capacity-limit error string.

self_reported_concerns: MAJ-SAFE-001 requires operator approval of a malicious registry PR — CODEOWNERS is a real gate and socially-engineering @jrnb2024 is non-trivial. Nevertheless the finding stands: estate doctrine (feedback_recursive_adversarial_review.md) mandates defence-in-depth, and a single human approval gate with no automated schema-level or runtime enforcement is insufficient for a trust-model invariant this load-bearing. The inline-fix is low-cost (one regex + five lines of Python) and must precede any real adopter onboarding.

I was unable to verify the correctness of the SHA pins on the five SHA-pinned actions (actions/checkout, actions/setup-python, actions/upload-artifact, actions/download-artifact, peter-evans/create-pull-request) against their published release tags, as this requires internet access outside this review scope. Any supply-chain attack via a compromised SHA-pinned action in the aggregate job could tamper with the index before upload. I assume the SHA pins were verified at authoring time per the existing D-038 supply-chain hash-pinning policy (020M). This assumption should be confirmed by the correctness reviewer (R2) cross-referencing the action SHA pins against published release manifests.

The `yaml.safe_load` → jsonschema validation pipeline is correctly ordered. No YAML deserialization attack surface exists. The `subprocess.run` arg-list pattern (no shell=True) throughout the Python script means no shell injection from registry-sourced values (`repo`, `default_branch`, `expected_scp_workflow_ref`). A `default_branch` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `$()`, `` ` ``) is passed as a literal argument to gh CLI, which returns an API error recorded as `unreachable`. These safety properties are strongly upheld in the current implementation.

The dual `additionalProperties: false` enforcement — first on the emit schema (scorecard-emit.schema.json) at step 4 of the aggregator loop, then on the index schema (scorecard-index.schema.json) after the loop — provides robust prevention of waiver-content leakage (reason, approved_by, waiver_id). An adversarial emit with extra fields in `waivers_aggregate` would be rejected at step 4 with `verification_failure` status. The never-waiver-content invariant is intact against schema-level attack vectors.

The emit['commit'] field (self-reported in the artifact) is not cross-validated against `headSha` returned by `gh run list`. However, since `emit['commit']` is NOT passed through to the index (the aggregator uses `last_emit_commit = head_sha` from the trusted API), this discrepancy has no effect on index integrity. The `ref` field is passed through from the emit and is not cross-validated against the run's branch, but it is informational only and does not gate any security decision in the aggregator or downstream consumers.
